r-9.1-plan-resource.title: 9.1 Plan Resource Management: OBS, RBS, RAM/RACI, organisational theory, resource management plan, team charter
r-9.1-plan-resource.notes: Agile context: in high-variability projects collaborative teams are critical (less time for central tasking); resource planning is less predictable, so fast-supply agreements and lean methods are critical for cost and schedule. Process: define how to estimate, acquire, manage and use team and physical resources; key benefit: approach and level of management effort based on project type and complexity; once or at predefined points. Ensures sufficient resources, considering availability of and competition for scarce resources, internal or procured; competing projects may affect cost, schedule, risk and quality. Inputs: charter (description, requirements, key stakeholders, summary milestones, preapproved financial resources); plan (quality management plan - resources needed for the quality level and metrics; scope baseline - deliverables drive resource types and quantities); documents (project schedule - timeline for resources; requirements documentation; risk register; stakeholder register - stakeholders interested in resources or able to influence resource choice); EEFs (culture and structure, geographic distribution, existing competencies and availability, marketplace); OPAs (HR policies, physical resource policies, safety and security policies, templates, historical information). Tools: expert judgment (negotiating for the best resources, talent management, preliminary effort level, reporting requirements, acquisition lead times, acquisition/retention/release risks, government and union regulations, seller and logistics management); data representation - goal: each work package has an unambiguous owner and everyone understands their role; hierarchical charts: WBS (deliverables to work packages, high-level areas of responsibility), organisational breakdown structure (OBS - arranged by existing departments, units or teams with their work packages listed, so a department sees all its project responsibilities), resource breakdown structure (hierarchical list of team and physical resources by category and type for planning, managing and controlling work); responsibility assignment matrix (RAM - resources assigned to each work package; high-level RAMs for groups per WBS component, lower-level ones for specific activities; shows all activities for one person and all people for one activity; ensures only one person is accountable for any task); RACI chart (responsible, accountable, consult, inform; useful with internal and external resources; Figure 9-4 verified: Create charter - Ann A, Ben R, Carlos I, Dina I, Ed I; Collect requirements - Ann I, Ben A, Carlos R, Dina C, Ed C; Submit change request - Ann I, Ben A, Carlos R, Dina R, Ed C; Develop test plan - Ann A, Ben C, Carlos I, Dina I, Ed R - note exactly one A per activity while R can be shared); text-oriented formats (position descriptions, role-responsibility-authority forms; reusable templates); organisational theory (how people, teams and units behave; can shorten planning time and effort; may recommend a flexible leadership style adapting to the team's maturity across the life cycle; organisation structure and culture shape the project organisation); meetings. Outputs: resource management plan (how resources are categorised, allocated, managed and released; may split into team management and physical resource management plans): identification of resources; acquiring resources; roles and responsibilities - role (function, e.g., civil engineer, business analyst, testing coordinator), authority (rights to apply resources, make decisions, sign approvals, accept deliverables, influence others - members work best when authority matches responsibility), responsibility (assigned duties and work), competence (skill and capacity; mismatches handled by training, hiring, schedule or scope changes); project organisation charts (team members and reporting relationships, detail scaled to the project - e.g., a 3,000-person disaster response team vs a 20-person internal project); project team resource management (define, staff, manage, release); training strategies; team development methods; resource control (physical resources available as needed, acquisition optimised, inventory, equipment, supplies); recognition plan (which rewards and when). Team charter: team values, communication guidelines, decision-making criteria and process, conflict resolution process, meeting guidelines, team agreements; sets expectations of acceptable behaviour; early commitment reduces misunderstandings and raises productivity; works best when the team develops or contributes to it; all members share responsibility for following it; reviewed periodically and used to orient new members. Document updates: assumption log (physical resource availability, logistics, location; team skills and availability), risk register. Data flow: charter from 4.1.

r-9.2-estimate-resources.title: 9.2 Estimate Activity Resources: resource calendars, estimating methods, resource requirements, RBS
r-9.2-estimate-resources.notes: Estimate team resources and the type and quantities of materials, equipment and supplies; key benefit: type, quantity and characteristics of resources required; periodically as needed. Closely coordinated with Estimate Costs (e.g., hire a consultant for local building codes vs internal labour; get automated assembly know-how via consultant, seminar or a manufacturing team member). Inputs: plan (resource management plan - how to identify and quantify resources per activity; scope baseline); documents (activity attributes - primary data source: resource requirements, imposed dates, location, assumptions, constraints; activity list; assumption log - productivity, availability, costs, approaches; cost estimates - affect quantity and skill choices; resource calendars - working days, shifts, business hours, weekends, holidays and periods when each resource is available, with experience, skill level and location; risk register); EEFs (resource location, availability, team skills, culture, published estimating data, marketplace); OPAs (staffing policies, supplies and equipment policies, historical resource information). Tools: expert judgment; bottom-up estimating (estimate at activity level and aggregate to work packages, control accounts and project); analogous estimating (quick, from a similar project, when only the top WBS levels are known); parametric estimating (e.g., 4,000 hours of coding to finish in 1 year at 2,000 hours per person per year = 2 coders); alternatives analysis (skill levels, machine sizes or types, manual vs automated tools, make-rent-buy); PMIS (resource management software for pools, RBS, availability, rates, calendars); meetings (with functional managers on resources per activity, level of effort, skill level, material quantities). Outputs: resource requirements (types and quantities per work package or activity, aggregated up the WBS, with assumptions); basis of estimates (method, sources, assumptions, constraints, range, confidence, risks); resource breakdown structure (hierarchical representation of resources by category - labour, material, equipment, supplies - and type - skill level, grade, certifications; guided categorisation in planning, now a completed document used to acquire and monitor resources; Figure 9-7 generic example: project -> personnel/material/equipment -> roles/levels/grades); document updates (activity attributes, assumption log - types and quantities and constraints such as collective bargaining agreements, continuous hours of operation, planned leave; lessons learned).

r-9.3-acquire-resources.title: 9.3 Acquire Resources: negotiation, pre-assignment, virtual teams, selection criteria, assignments and resource calendars
r-9.3-acquire-resources.notes: Obtain team members, facilities, equipment, materials, supplies and other resources; key benefit: guides selection and assignment of resources to activities; periodically as needed. Internal resources are assigned by functional or resource managers; external ones come through procurement. The PM team may lack direct control over selection (collective bargaining, subcontractor personnel, matrix environment, reporting relationships). Considerations: negotiate and influence those who provide resources; failing to acquire them affects schedule, budget, satisfaction, quality and risk, and may cancel the project; if unavailable, alternative resources with different competencies or costs may be used provided no legal, regulatory or mandatory criteria are violated - plan for this and document impacts on schedule, budget, risk, quality, training and other plans. Inputs: plan (resource management plan; procurement management plan - resources from outside and integration of procurement; cost baseline - overall budget); documents (project schedule - when resources are needed; resource calendars - availability, time zones, work hours, vacations, local holidays, maintenance schedules, other commitments; progressively elaborated; resource requirements; stakeholder register - expectations for specific resources); EEFs (resource availability, competence, experience and costs; marketplace; structure; geography); OPAs (acquisition and assignment policies, historical information). Tools: decision making - multicriteria decision analysis with weighted selection criteria (availability, cost, ability; for team members also experience, knowledge of the customer and environment, skills with project tools, attitude to teamwork, international factors such as location, time zone and communication capability); interpersonal skills - negotiation with functional managers (best resources for the needed time), other project teams (share scarce or specialised resources) and external organisations and suppliers (respect their policies and legal criteria); ability to influence and organisational politics matter (e.g., stressing project visibility to a functional manager); pre-assignment (resources determined in advance - named in a competitive proposal, project depends on specific experts, or assigned during chartering before the resource plan exists); virtual teams (groups with a shared goal who spend little or no time face to face; enable geographically spread teams, remote experts, home-based workers, different shifts, people with mobility limitations or disabilities, projects otherwise stopped by travel cost, savings on offices and equipment; communication planning becomes more important - time to set expectations, facilitate communication, conflict protocols, inclusive decisions, cultural understanding, shared credit). Outputs: physical resource assignments (material, equipment, supplies, locations); project team assignments (members, roles and responsibilities, team directory, names in org charts and schedules); resource calendars; change requests; plan updates (resource management plan, cost baseline); document updates (lessons learned, project schedule, RBS, resource requirements, risk register, stakeholder register); EEF updates (resource availability, consumable resources used); OPA updates (acquisition and assignment documentation). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.
